title: The P3 sweet spot for housing projects
summary: Here, Melissa Buck summarizes insights from a recent discussion on the potential of public-private partnerships (P3s) to address workforce housing needs.
body_text: In a recent discussion with more than one hundred city managers around Colorado, I explored the potential of public-private partnerships (P3s) in addressing workforce housing needs. Many communities are grappling with acute housing shortages, particularly middle-income households (typically those making 60% to 120% of area median income, such as teachers, entry-level professionals, and first responders). Here, I summarize key insights from this discussion, focusing on the “sweet spot” for P3 housing projects in terms of size and procurement approach. Why a P3? The ideal P3 project leverages the strengths of both public and private sectors. Usually, they are structured so risks such as construction delays, cost overruns, and regulatory changes are allocated to the sector best able to address them. For example, in the most classic P3 model, the private side leads a facility’s design, construction, financing, operation, and maintenance. Municipalities usually start exploring P3 options when projects feature one or more of these characteristics: Funding is insufficient: The project requires more funding than is available from public sources. Urgency: The project is urgently needed in the community. Risk sharing: The project involves significant financial, operational, or market-related risks that can be shared with a private partner. Revenue generation: The project generates revenue, such as tenant rents, that can be used to pay debt service, compensate the private partner, and/or be leveraged to create more projects. What kind of P3 project works for housing? Different P3 models vary in the level of private involvement and risk transfer. Here’s a rank-ordered list of procurement models from maximum to minimum private involvement. Design-Build-Finance-Operate-Maintain (DBFOM). The private party designs, builds, finances, operates, and maintains the project and the municipality repays all of these costs over time either through a revenue share or periodic availability payments based on performance. Design-Build-Operate-Maintain (DBOM). The private party designs, builds, operates, and maintains the project and the municipality finances the project, typically using low-cost tax-exempt municipal bonds. Design-Build Finance (DBF). The private sector designs, builds, and finances the project, turning it over to the municipality upon completion. Design-Build (DB). The private sector designs and builds the project. The local government finances, operates, and maintains the asset. Design-Bid-Build (DBB). The most classic public procurement model where the municipality designs the project, solicits bids for construction, and, generally speaking, the lowest bid wins the contract. Notably, this procurement model tends to have the least amount of cost efficiencies. At the top is the classic P3 approach, which maximizes private involvement, risk transfer, and cost efficiencies to the private entity. As one works down the list, the level of private involvement (and risk) drops. While the DBFOM model is successful in large infrastructure projects, it often doesn’t fit the scale of most community housing projects, which typically require at least 250-300 housing units to be economically viable. Therefore, the DBOM approach, where the public entity retains financing responsibilities, is often more suitable for housing projects. The DBOM approach A DBOM model may work better than DBFOM for workforce housing solutions for several key reasons, including: Lower cost of capital DBOM: The public sector retains responsibility for financing, often allowing access to cheaper capital through municipal bonds or other public financing options, thus reducing the overall cost of the project. DBFOM: The private sector finances the project, typically at higher interest rate than tax-exempt municipal bonds, which can increase the overall project cost. Risk management DBOM: While the public sector retains some financial risk, it can leverage its creditworthiness and access to lower-cost capital to manage these risks more effectively. DBFOM: Shifts more financial risk to the private sector, which might demand higher returns to compensate for this risk, potentially increasing costs (and the amount the local government will repay the developer). Transparency and accountability DBOM: Municipal bond financings often come with greater transparency and accountability requirements, which can enhance public trust and ensure the project meets public sector standards. DBFOM: Private financing can sometimes reduce transparency and accountability, as private entities may not be subject to the same scrutiny as public agencies. All told, a DBOM model may work better for many middle-income housing projects because the public sector can leverage its financing advantages, maintain greater control and oversight, and ensure better alignment with community needs, goals, and transparency requirements. A potential sweet spot We believe the following project profile is an ideal candidate for a DBOM P3 approach because it would be financially viable and attract a sufficient number of developers to bid on the project. Number of units: 250+ Most developers are looking for economies of scale and revenue generation because it helps ensure the project is financially viable. Unit size and mix: Market-driven; typically, studio – 3 bedroom A mix of unit sizes caters to a diverse range of households, enhancing market appeal and occupancy rates. Affordability levels: Middle income Aside from addressing a crucial gap in the housing market, middle-income tenants typically have more stable incomes compared to lower-income households, reducing the risk of rental defaults and helping ensure consistent revenue streams. Location and site selection: Level / flat already identified This reduces site preparation costs and simplifies the construction process, which can accelerate the project timeline and minimize unforeseen expenses. Design and amenities: Unique to market High-quality design and desirable amenities (e.g. fitness centers, communal spaces, green areas) enhance tenant satisfaction and retention. Financing/Funding sources: Project specific Basically, a tailored financial solution to meet each project’s unique needs, which can include a mix of public funds, private investments, grants, and tax incentives. Of course, as with any P3 project, success hinges on developing clear objectives, allocating risk appropriately, ensuring financial viability, and emphasizing community engagement. This also doesn’t mean a smaller project couldn’t be done as a DBOM P3 (of course it could). However, by meeting these criteria, a middle-income housing project becomes a viable and attractive solution for addressing workforce housing needs, benefitting both the community and private partners involved. title: Do Employers Actually Care About a Multi-Year Career Gap in 2026? A Recruiter's Honest Answer
summary: Returning to work after years off? A recruiter's honest take on whether a multi-year gap really hurts, the myths to drop, and what gets you hired back.
body_text: Do employers actually care about a multi-year career gap in 2026? Mostly, no. A gap you can explain in one honest sentence is rarely what sinks a candidacy. What a recruiter actually checks is narrower than the fear you are carrying: the reason you stepped away, how current your skills are, and how ready you are to do the job now. The years off are not a moral verdict on you. An unexplained gap sitting next to skills that went stale is the real problem, and both of those are fixable before you ever hit apply. Here is the thing nobody tells you when you are staring at four blank years on a resume. The gap feels like a scarlet letter. To the person reading your application, it is usually a single line of curiosity, answered in a moment, and forgotten. You have probably been told the opposite so many times you believe it in your bones. That any break longer than a few months makes you damaged goods. That recruiters toss your resume the second they spot the missing year. That you either hide the whole thing or grovel for it. Some of that fear is earned; the job market can be brutal and some hiring is genuinely closed-minded. Most of it is inherited panic that does not match how experienced people actually hire in 2026. This is not a how-to on formatting a gap resume. We have detailed guides for that mechanics part, and they are linked throughout. This is the honest answer to the question underneath the formatting question: does the gap really matter, and are you still hireable? Short version, from the recruiter's side of the table: yes you are, and here is what they are truly weighing. The fear versus what actually happens The fear runs on a loop. A gap means you could not hold a job, or that something is wrong with you, or that you will get auto-rejected before a human ever sees your name. People describe it as a death spiral, and it feels exactly like that when you are inside it. Now the other side. Ask people who have hired hundreds or thousands of employees what a multi-year gap does to a candidate, and the answer is remarkably flat. A break to travel does not read as a red flag. Time out to raise kids does not read as a red flag. A layoff during a bad stretch for your industry does not read as a red flag. What reads as a flag is silence, the kind that makes a stranger fill in the blank with the worst possible story. The pandemic did a lot of quiet work here. Between 2020 and 2022 millions of people caught a gap they did not choose. Whole industries froze. A recruiter who flinches at "I was out during the shutdowns" is telling on themselves. Gaps stopped being exotic. They became the median. None of this means gaps are invisible. They get noticed. Noticed is not the same as disqualifying, and the difference between the two is almost entirely in your hands. What a recruiter actually does with a gap Strip away the anxiety and a recruiter is running three checks when they see time off. None of them is a judgment on your character. Check one: why? They are mostly making sure you did not get quietly fired and are now papering over it. A clean reason and a sense that you left your last role on decent terms resolves this in a sentence. If a former manager or colleague would speak well of you, the "why" question basically answers itself. Check two: are your skills current? This is the legitimate one, and it is the concern people underrate the most. A hiring manager in a fast-moving field will worry that during your two or four years away, the tools moved and you did not. Expired certifications. A codebase or platform you have never touched. A vague "I will pick it up in a few months" when the role needs someone who can contribute now. This worry is fair, and it is the single most useful thing to disarm ahead of time. Check three: can you do this job today? Everything funnels to this. A gap plus a convincing signal that you are current and ready beats a spotless timeline plus rust. Hiring is triage with thin information, so anything left unexplained gets treated as a risk. Your job is to make sure nothing about your time off is left for a stranger to guess at. Notice what is not on that list. Nobody is grading you on how much you "deserved" the break, or how productive you stayed every single week, or whether the story wraps up neatly. A good hire is someone who can do the work and will stick around, and a gap tells a recruiter almost nothing about either until you give it context. If your applications are vanishing and you suspect the timeline is why, our teardown of why resumes actually get rejected walks through the flaws that genuinely cost you, most of which have nothing to do with the gap. Myth 1: a gap makes you unhireable False, and the counterexamples are everywhere once you look. A parent returns after four years and lands a role. Someone takes a year to travel and walks back into their field. A caregiver steps out for two years for a sick relative and gets hired without a raised eyebrow. There are people who spent seventeen years out of paid work, for kids or their own illness or both, and found paid work again in their late fifties, through networking and a free re-employment course and a rehearsed one-line answer. Read those stories closely and none of them got hired by hiding the gap. They got hired by explaining it plainly and pairing it with proof they were ready. "Unhireable" is a story the gap tells you at 2 a.m. It is not a story a competent recruiter tells about you when you give them something better to work with. The 2026 caveat, said honestly: the market is genuinely hard in some corners right now, and that is not about your gap. Some fields have a glut of candidates and a wave of layoffs to absorb. If you are getting silence, it may be the market, not the missing year. That is a reason to reactivate your skills and lean on people who know you, not a reason to conclude you are finished. Myth 2: you must hide it or fudge the dates This is the tempting one, and it is the one that gets people in real trouble. Stretch the end date of your last job to swallow the gap. Invent a consulting stint. Spin up an LLC and claim you were self-employed the whole time. The internet is full of these tricks, and they feel clever right up until they do not. The same line runs through job titles, where reframing versus lying splits the safe edits from the ones verification catches. Here is the mechanism that catches them. Employment dates are verifiable, and not only through a friendly former HR department. A large chunk of US employment history flows through The Work Number, an Equifax-run database that many payroll systems feed automatically. A background check can pull your real start and end dates from it whether or not your old company still exists as a place to call. To keep your history out of it, you have to actively opt out with Equifax. So the padded date that looked airtight on your resume can quietly contradict the verification report, and now the conversation is not about your gap. It is about your honesty, which is a far worse conversation to be having after an offer. There is a clean line worth holding onto. Choosing what to include is not the same as fabricating what is not true. You are allowed to lead with your strengths, group your experience so a break does not dominate the page, and skip ancient irrelevant jobs. You are not allowed to invent an employer or move dates you cannot defend. One of those is editing; the other is a landmine that goes off during verification. If you want the safe version of "make the gap less prominent," that is a structural choice, and our guide to the career-gap resume plus the functional and combination formats shows you how to do it without lying. Myth 3: you must over-explain and apologize The opposite failure. People swing so hard into transparency that they turn a non-issue into a spotlight. They open with the gap, apologize for it, then narrate the whole difficult chapter in the first thirty seconds, unprompted, and watch the interviewer's face tighten. You need one sentence. Honest, brief, forward-facing, delivered without a flinch. Something in the shape of: "I stepped away from paid work to care for my family, that is resolved now, and I am ready to get back to it." Then you stop talking and let them move to the next question, which they almost always do. The confidence in the delivery matters more than the words. A candidate who states the reason calmly and pivots to the future signals exactly the steadiness a hiring manager is hoping to see. A candidate who spirals into justification signals the opposite, no matter how sympathetic the reason. Brevity is not evasion. It is respect for the fact that your break is a normal part of a life, not a confession. The interview-side version of this, with more scripts for the actual conversation, lives in our guide to explaining career gaps during an interview . Not sure how your gap is reading to a recruiter? Run your resume through a free review and see the flags a hiring manager would notice first, gap included, before you send it out. Get a free resume review → The one honest line for the common reasons You do not need a script for every twist your life took. You need one steady framing for the category your gap falls into. A few that land well, all built on the same honest-plus-brief-plus-forward spine. Caregiving, for a child or a parent or a partner. "I took time out of paid work to care for my family. That season is behind us, and I am glad to be coming back." No pictures, no diagnosis, no timeline of the hard days. Caregiving is one of the most common reasons a competent adult steps away, and most people across a hiring table have either done it or watched someone close to them do it. A layoff or a rough market. Name it plainly and move on. "My role was cut when the company downsized in 2024, and it took a while to find the right next thing rather than just the next thing." Layoffs are not a character flaw and everyone knows it. Health, yours or a family member's. You can name the category without the details. "I stepped back for health reasons, that is resolved, and I have been getting current again in the field." You are under no obligation to disclose a diagnosis to a hiring manager, and disclosing the category is usually enough to close the topic. Use your own judgment on how much to share and with whom; this is not legal advice, just a practical framing. A deliberate sabbatical or travel. Own it as a choice, not an accident. "I planned a year to travel while I had the window, and I am back and focused." Framed as intent, this often reads as someone who sets goals and executes them, which is not a bad first impression. Whatever the reason, the coaching is the same. Tell the truth, keep it to a breath or two, and land on why you are ready now. Skill recency: the thing that actually moves the needle If check two, "are your skills current," is the real concern, then reactivating your skills is the real fix. Of everything a returner can do, this one pays back the most, and it sits almost entirely within your control. You do not need a second degree. You need a recent, provable signal that you are back in the field and current on how it works today. A short course with a certificate. A freelance project or two, even small ones. Volunteer work that used the muscles the job will use. A portfolio built from public data or a personal project, sized to the roles you are targeting. The mechanism matters more than the scale. A hiring manager who sees a class you finished last quarter and a small project you shipped stops worrying that you are two years behind, because the evidence says you are not. The sharpest version of this, straight from people who hire: pull three or four job descriptions for the exact role you want, list the skills they keep asking for, and build your recent activity to match that list. If a data role wants SQL and a scripting language, learn enough to ship something small in both and put it where they can see it. You are not trying to relearn everything. You are trying to close the specific gap between your last paid title and the next one. Volunteer and community work from your time off is real experience, not filler. Coordinating a school program, running a nonprofit's books, managing a fundraiser, organizing a team of parents; these carry skills and, often, references. Our guide to putting volunteer work on a resume and the piece on framing transferable skills cover how to translate that into language a recruiter reads as competence. Networking beats the apply button for returners If you take one tactical thing from this piece, take this. For someone re-entering after years away, cold applications are the hardest possible path, and a warm introduction is the easiest. This is not a motivational cliche. It is a structural fact about how re-entry actually works. A cold resume with a gap has to survive a stranger's snap judgment. A resume that arrives with "my friend vouches for this person" arrives with the gap already contextualized and the trust already borrowed. The people who get back in fastest after a long break almost always got there through someone who knew them, not through the two-hundredth application into a portal. So start with your old colleagues, your former managers who liked you, the parents and neighbors and acquaintances who work at places you would work. Tell them plainly that you are coming back and what you are aiming for. Let a real person carry your name past the filter that a gap would otherwise trip. To understand exactly where in the pipeline a referral changes your odds, our walkthrough of how hiring actually works maps the stages a returner most needs to skip. Use LinkedIn's Career Break feature instead of a scary blank LinkedIn built a tool specifically for this, and it is underused. Since March 2022 you can add a Career Break to your profile, and as of 2026 it sits in your Experience section like any other entry rather than leaving an ominous empty stretch on your timeline. You add it through Add profile section, then the Core menu, then Add career break. There are around thirteen labels to choose from, including caregiving and health and well-being, plus options like parental leave, travel, bereavement, relocation, and reskilling; you can also leave the type blank and describe it yourself. Adding one is a routine profile edit, and like any edit, whether it lands in your network's feed is governed by your profile-update-visibility setting, so it does not have to broadcast your break. LinkedIn's menu wording drifts over time, so if the path looks slightly different when you go in, hunt around the same profile-section area. Why bother? Because it turns an unexplained absence into a labeled, ordinary chapter, and it lets you write a line or two about what you did or learned. LinkedIn's own position is that giving hirers context about a break makes you easier to reach out to, which lines up with everything else in this piece: the silence is the problem, and this feature fills it. It is not magic and it will not overcome stale skills on its own. Paired with a reactivation story, it removes one more thing for a recruiter to guess about. Returnships: the on-ramp built for exactly this If your break ran long and the thought of competing head-on with continuously-employed candidates feels grim, returnships exist for precisely that gap. A returnship is a paid, fixed-term program, often a few months, aimed at experienced people coming back after time away. Think of it as an internship for adults with a track record, designed to get you current and often leading to a full role. Large employers run them, sometimes labeled returnship or returner program, across tech, finance, and other fields. They are competitive and not everywhere, but they solve the returner's chicken-and-egg problem head on: you cannot get current without a role, and you cannot get a role without being current. A returnship hands you both. We cover which programs exist and how to apply in the guide to returnship programs , so treat this section as the nudge and that one as the map. When a gap genuinely is a hurdle, and what to do Reassurance without honesty is useless, so here is the honest part. There are real situations where a gap does become a live obstacle, and pretending otherwise would not help you. The first is a long gap in a field that moved fast while you were out. Tech, some corners of marketing, anything where the tools turn over every couple of years. A seventeen-year absence and a single fresh certificate will not, on its own, land you a senior engineering or PM role in a field that reinvented its stack twice since you left. That is not a moral failing. It is a skills-currency gap, and pretending it away only wastes the applications you fire off before you have closed it. The second is a long gap with no reactivation story at all, dropped into a crowded market. Out for years, have not touched the field, applying cold against a flood of laid-off candidates who never left it. In some fields in 2026, that pile is deep enough that even people with unbroken timelines are hearing crickets. So the silence you are getting might be that specific stack of conditions, not the missing year by itself. The fix for both is reactivation, not a cover-up, and sometimes a target you can actually hit this quarter. Learn the exact tools the postings keep naming. Ship one small thing that proves you can use them. And if the honest match for what you can demonstrate right now is a rung below where you left, take the rung. A junior-ish role that gets you back on payroll and back around the current tools beats holding out for a title your last six months of work cannot back up. From there you move up quicker than the fear predicts, because you spent years building the base and only a little while off it. The mindset: you are not behind One last thing, because the fear gets this part most wrong. A break is a period, not a permanent condition. The skills you built before you left did not evaporate the day you stopped clocking in. They went quiet. And quiet skills wake up a lot faster than brand-new ones get built from scratch, which is the whole reason a returner with real prior experience is a different bet than a fresh grad. The people who struggle most walk into the room already apologizing, already carrying themselves like a liability the employer is being generous to consider. A recruiter reads that posture almost instantly, and it does more damage than the gap ever could. The ones who do well name the reason in a sentence, point to the class they finished last quarter, and talk about the next role like a normal next step rather than a rescue mission. Same resume. Same gap. The read on the person flips completely. You made a choice, or life made one for you, and you took the time. Now you show up with a reactivated skill set and a one-line answer you can deliver without your voice wobbling. Nobody in that room is looking at a person to pity. They are looking at someone who set a plan, handled whatever the years threw at them, and came back and did the work to get current, which happens to be most of what any hire is really being asked to prove. Frequently Asked Questions Will a multi-year gap get my resume auto-rejected before a human sees it? Almost never for the gap by itself. The software up front is matching keywords and hard requirements. It is not scanning for blank months and bouncing you. When a returner does get filtered, the culprit is usually a resume light on the current skills and exact terms the posting asks for. So the fix is not hiding the timeline. It is loading the page with the recent, relevant proof the filter and the human both want. Is there such a thing as a gap that is "too long"? No magic cutoff exists. Weirdly, three months and five years land in roughly the same place once you attach a clear reason and some proof you are current. What a longer break does is sharpen the skills question, nothing more. Two years out of a fast field needs a bigger reactivation story than six months out. Length is a dial on how much you invest in showing currency, not a wall. Should I just leave the gap unexplained and hope they don't ask? No. Silence is the version that actually costs you, because a stranger fills it with the worst thing they can imagine, whether that is prison, a firing for cause, or something worse. None of that is you, but the blank invites the guess. You do not owe anyone your life story. You do want one calm sentence ready, and often a short line on the resume or LinkedIn naming the reason, so nobody has to invent one. Is it really that risky to fudge my dates to cover the gap? Yes. Here is why it bites. Employment dates get verified, and not just by phoning your old boss. A big share of US payroll flows into The Work Number, an Equifax database a background check can query for your actual start and end dates, whether or not that old company still picks up the phone. Your padded date then quietly contradicts the report. Now the topic is your honesty, which is a much worse thing to be defending after an offer than a gap ever was. What do I actually say when they ask about the gap in the interview? One honest, forward-facing sentence, then hush. "I stepped away to care for my family, that is behind us, and I am ready to get back to it." Done. Say it evenly, skip the apology, and let them steer to the next question, which they usually do within seconds. Tone carries this more than wording. A wobble reads as a problem; a steady delivery reads as a non-event. The full interview version is linked up in the piece. How do I make my skills look current after years off? Show fresh evidence, not assurances. A course you finished last quarter with the certificate to prove it. A couple of freelance projects, even tiny ones. Volunteer work that flexed the right muscles. A small portfolio aimed straight at the roles you want. The move that works: pull three or four real postings, write down the skills they keep repeating, and build your recent activity to hit exactly that list. Do that and you answer the currency question before an interviewer thinks to raise it. Does the LinkedIn Career Break feature actually help? It helps mainly by killing the mystery. Since March 2022 you can drop a Career Break into your Experience section, tagged caregiving, health and well-being, parental leave, travel, and about a dozen more, and like any profile edit its visibility to your network stays under your control. A scary blank becomes an ordinary, labeled chapter you get to describe in a line or two. On its own it will not fix rusty skills. Bolted onto a real reactivation story, it hands recruiters context where they used to get a guess. I was a stay-at-home parent. How do I structure a resume with no recent paid title? Lead with your strongest card, be that a degree you recently finished, relevant volunteer work, or a fresh course, and pick a format that keeps the break out of the headline. The nuts and bolts of that live in dedicated guides for stay-at-home-parent and caregiver resumes, plus the functional and combination formats linked above. The one-line truth: parenting is not the problem here, and the volunteer roles from those years are real experience, references included. Should I bring up a health or mental-health reason for the gap? That call is yours. You can name the category, "I stepped back for health reasons, and that is resolved," without ever handing over a diagnosis, and that usually closes the subject. No hiring manager is entitled to your medical history. Share what feels safe, with people you have some reason to trust, and keep the sentence pointed at what comes next rather than what you went through. Judgment call, not a rule, and there is no wrong answer that keeps you honest. The market feels impossible and I'm still getting silence. Is it the gap? Quite possibly not. A few fields in 2026 are genuinely swamped, layoffs stacked on a glut of applicants, and that silence is hitting people with unbroken timelines too. So before you pin it on the missing year, check two things. Do your skills read as current? And are you firing into portals instead of working the people who already know you? Reactivate, lean hard on that network, and look at a returnship. Any of those beats obsessing over the gap. title: Goodwood, Innit?
body_text: Creating the next generation of motorcycles Our vision Learn Latest news Collabs Custom builds Our vision Learn Latest news Collabs Custom builds Goodwood, Innit? LiveWire Takes on the Greatest Motorsport Garden Party on Earth Some events are races. Some are trade shows. Some are festivals. Goodwood Festival of Speed is all three, crammed into the rolling hills of West Sussex and turned up to eleven. For four days, the grounds of the Duke of Richmond's estate become a temporary capital of speed, where Formula 1 cars, prototype race machines, vintage motorcycles, million-dollar supercars, EVs, customs, choppers, and everything in between converge on a single hillclimb. It is somehow polished and completely bananas at the same time. A Little Bit of Everything One of the things that makes Goodwood special is its refusal to pick a team. Combustion and electric. Vintage and futuristic. Factory race teams and backyard builders. Hypercars and chopped motos. Walking through the event feels like scrolling through the world's most unhinged motorsports mood board. It's all here. For anyone who loves machines, Goodwood isn't just a show. It's sensory overload. As Max of Reload Land put it: “It’s the absolute overflow of dreams for any enthusiast. Everything you've imagined is there and you can basically touch it.” Up the Hill Of course, it wouldn't be Goodwood without the hillclimb. The 1.16-mile ribbon of pavement that cuts through the Goodwood estate isn't just the centerpiece of the Festival of Speed. It's sacred ground. Every manufacturer, race team, and driver arrives wanting their moment on that stretch of tarmac. The start line crackles with anticipation. Mechanics make last-minute adjustments. Supercars bark through rev limiters. Historic race bikes cough to life. Crowds pack every available viewing spot. Then, flags go down and one by one, machines launch toward the trees. In the middle of all that noise and spectacle, LiveWire's electric motorcycles delivered their own kind of drama. Aaron Guardado piloted the S2 Alpinista Corsa up the famed hill, demonstrating the kind of instant acceleration that can make even seasoned motorsport fans stop and take notice. While V12s and race engines announced themselves with thunderous noise, the LiveWire machines attacked the course with something different: an almost calm sense of urgency. No waiting. No hesitation. Just pure torque. As Aaron put it: “Fast AF, as per usual.” For spectators seeing the bikes in action before visiting the display, the hillclimb served as proof that these weren't simply motorcycles to admire behind a barrier. They were machines built to perform. The result was a steady stream of visitors arriving at the booth with curiosity. Charley Being Charley One of the biggest crowd-pleasers of the weekend came courtesy of an old friend of the brand: Charley Boorman. Long before he was charging up the Goodwood hill aboard a LiveWire, Charley helped introduce electric motorcycles to millions of viewers around the world in Long Way Up, the acclaimed adventure series in which he and longtime riding partner Ewan McGregor rode from Ushuaia, Argentina to Los Angeles aboard prototype LiveWire motorcycles. At the time, the idea of crossing continents on electric motorcycles felt impossible to many riders. Charley and Ewan proved otherwise, showcasing not only the capability of electric motorcycles, but the spirit of adventure behind them. That connection makes Charley's appearances with LiveWire feel more like family reunions than celebrity guest appearances. And true to form, he didn't disappoint. The veteran adventurer spent the weekend wandering the paddock, chatting with marshals, riders, and friends as if he'd known everyone there for decades. Which, frankly, he probably has. Then came the hill. Then came the summit. Then came the burnout. While everyone else was busy navigating procedures and waiting for instructions, Charley casually rolled into position and let the rear tire do some talking. And if there is a more fitting way to celebrate the partnership between one of motorcycling's greatest storytellers and one of motorcycling's most disruptive brands, we haven't found it yet. Enter the Honcho While the S2 lineup won people over with performance and design, the S4 Honcho won hearts. Kids climbed aboard and instantly started imagining adventures. Adults pictured rides around campgrounds, properties, neighborhoods, and weekend escapes. The Honcho Van became a magnet for curious attendees all weekend long. The Stuff You Can't Put on a Spec Sheet The funny thing about Goodwood is that the cars and motorcycles are only part of the story. It's the random conversations. The police officer who sat on the Alpinista and lit up like a kid. The children imagining electric motorcycles under the Christmas tree. The autograph seekers trying to determine whether members of the LiveWire team were actually famous. The England football match watched in England. The ice cream consumed while waiting at the start line. The mosquito attack that forced creative engineering solutions involving napkins, jacket sleeves, and eventually an electric bug zapper that became an unofficial team initiation device. These are the moments you remember long after the event goes quiet. Done By Enthusiasts Perhaps the best observation came from Max, who described Goodwood in three words: “Done by enthusiasts.” That's what makes the event special. It's built by people who genuinely love motorcycles, cars, racing, engineering, and all the wonderfully irrational reasons humans create machines that go faster than they need to. It's also what makes LiveWire feel at home there. Whether people arrived curious about EVs, searching for their next motorcycle, or simply looking for the coolest thing they'd see all weekend, the conversations, reactions, and smiles told the story. The people made the weekend. And after four scorching days, countless conversations, several hillclimb runs, more than a few laughs, and at least one mosquito-fueled survival exercise, the team packed up and headed home. Probably a couple pounds lighter. Definitely a few stories richer. See you next year, Goodwood. title: How Stunner grew from 7k to 85 million views with Photoroom
summary: Discover how Stunner rebuilt their business from scratch, using Photoroom to create studio-quality visuals, save time, and turn creativity into viral growth.
body_text: Life before Photoroom Relocated their business with no photography equipment Manually removed backgrounds, spending precious hours Inconsistent images made shirts look less appealing Creative projects stalled while they tried to fix basic visuals Life with Photoroom Clean product photos boost buyer confidence and sales Quick, one-tap background removal saves hours each week Freed time fuels creative visuals, hitting 85M+ views on Instagram No costly studio needed - two shirt sales covers their Photoroom yearly subscription Reinvests savings and energy into filming matches, hosting events, and expanding the brand In 2017, Polina discovered something surprising when she first moved in with Serge: a small mountain of vintage football shirts crammed into every corner of their new shared flat. Serge had been collecting these pieces of football history for years, and his ever-growing stash was on the brink of taking over their home. Neither of them imagined at the time that this shared love for football (and its iconic shirts) would become a business that would survive war, displacement, and countless obstacles—only to flourish in a brand-new city. An unexpected calling What started as a simple plan to list the football shirts on eBay turned into something bigger as soon as Polina’s creative vision took hold. Rather than simply photographing shirts laid out on the floor, she styled them into everyday outfits, took film photos, and began to share their uniqueness online. Sales trickled in, and then picked up. By 2019, they had established Stunner , a vintage football shirt brand operating out of Kyiv, Ukraine. They opened a physical store to connect with customers. They dreamed of improving their store and growing their business beyond sales. Then, in February 2022, mere hours before missiles fell on Kyiv, Polina and Serge left Ukraine with nothing more than a two-week plan to visit a friend for business in Brussels. They never returned home. New city, new challenges Once it became clear they couldn’t return safely to Kyiv, the couple faced the hardest choice of their lives: abandon their old life or try to rebuild from scratch. Family and friends in Ukraine encouraged them to stay abroad, stay safe, and keep Stunner alive. All their professional equipment stayed behind in Kyiv: mannequins, lights, backdrops, everything. Even worse, most of their vintage shirts were either stored or sold off so they could afford basic living costs on the road. “We lost everything, our store, our flat, and most of our stock. Suddenly, we were abroad with 40 football shirts and no plans.” – Polina Vynohradova, Co-founder, Stunner Media From Brussels to Italy and finally to Manchester, Polina and Serge found themselves improvising constantly to replenish their stock and keep their love for football alive. They added new creative dimensions to Stunner, filming live football matches and covering local clubs. When they finally settled in Manchester, they took the biggest leap yet: opening a second physical store. But with a new store comes new challenges. “Back in Kyiv, we had a routine, proper lighting, all the gear. In Manchester, we invested everything into just having the store and had nothing left for photography.” – Serge Shcherbyna, Co-founder, Stunner Media They also wanted to turn their new store into a community space that celebrated football culture in new ways. “We wanted more than just a store. We wanted to create a football hub that doubled as an oasis of culture and creativity. A space where we could make screenings, art, and exhibitions for fans and creators.” – Polina Vynohradova, Co-founder, Stunner Media With limited funds and no equipment, they needed a tool to capture inventory and a visual sense of community for their website and social media, without compromising on quality. With this, they set out to find the perfect solution. Rebuilding Stunner’s creative vision, with Photoroom The couple tried some apps before discovering Photoroom. “The results didn’t always look good. They were not exactly website material. And it also took a very long time to process everything manually,” Polina shares. They’ve stuck with Photoroom for a few reasons: Accurate background removal Polina and Serge immediately loved Photoroom’s precision. Unlike other apps, “Photoroom easily removes background from our photos and gives the most clear results even for intricate objects like my hair, which is fluffy,” shares Polina, adding that “Other apps just remove parts of my hair and make me look semi-bald.” Having a one-stop creative toolkit With about 200 shirts in stock, Photoroom’s easy background removal and AI-powered attention to detail lets them replicate the slick look of a studio shoot, without actually needing one. Polina and Serge also use Photoroom to layer backgrounds and motion blur effects to produce eye-catching visuals. Fresh creative content As Stunner pivoted toward short, engaging content, Photoroom unlocked a new level of creativity. Polina recalls making one reel for Stunner’s Instagram using Photoroom for the special effect: “It went viral. We gained 67,000 views in 24 hours, and people kept asking how we achieved that smooth effect. Photoroom, of course!” “We needed a tool to easily remove background from our photos, and Photoroom has been very handy from the beginning. It’s still a critical part of our content creation process, for editing our product photos and creative reels for Instagram.” – Serge Shcherbyna, Co-founder, Stunner Media Stunner today: time saved, a community built Despite opening during a chaotic time in their lives, Stunner’s second store has become a true community hub, hosting exhibitions, screenings, and even offering free workspace to local artists. Polina and Serge keep stunning their audience with beautiful visuals, using Photoroom as their trusted visual partner that: Skyrockets social media engagement Stunner’s Instagram reels, many of which involve Photoroom’s effects, have collectively pulled in 85 million views in one year—an unimaginable number for a small, two-person outfit that previously gained about 7,000 views. Saves money on product visuals Armed with Photoroom, Stunner now creates freely without overspending. As Serge shares, “Renting a studio or pro lighting would be costly. But selling two shirts covers our Photoroom yearly subscription. It’s a healthy exchange of investment.” Builds trust with aesthetics Clear, consistent images on their website help customers feel confident ordering online. Serge points out, “High-quality product photos show we care about each piece, and that builds trust right away.” Saves time for creative freedom Freed from the grunt work of manual photo editing, the couple have time to travel, cover more matches, and keep producing inventive content. “Every new feature in Photoroom pushes our creativity further,” says Polina. “Photoroom is so good that it’s boosted my capabilities as a creative business owner. I can look at all these tools in the app, experiment with them, and they’ll trigger an idea I never thought I had.” – Polina Vynohradova, Co-founder, Stunner Media Looking ahead Polina and Serge admit they aren’t big on five-year plans—life taught them how quickly everything can change. But one thing’s certain: Stunner will keep adapting and experimenting, sharing vintage football culture with fans far and wide. For the couple who left Kyiv with nothing but 40 shirts, Stunner is more than a business. It’s a testament to resilience, creativity, and the power of community. And with Photoroom in their pockets and a fresh wave of viral reels on deck, Stunner is poised to keep inspiring football lovers and small business dreamers around the world. “If you’re just starting out your business, or even if you’ve lost everything, keep going and don’t be afraid to take risks. Small steps build big futures. That’s how we’ve rebuilt, one day at a time.” – Polina and Serge, founders of Stunner Media Keep up with Polina and Serge’s work with the Stunner store on Instagram .

title: From Possibility to Impact: Perspectives on World Quantum Day 2026
summary: On World Quantum Day 2026, D-Wave leads the quantum computing race with real-world commercial impact and leadership across annealing & gate-model technologies.
body_text: Article Highlights While the quantum computing field is expanding, not all players are on equal footing. D-Wave has already delivered commercially valuable quantum systems with real-world impact. As organizations begin to push against the limits of classical computing, quantum is emerging as a practical complement today, not just a future promise. The State of Quantum Computing in 2026 Last week, Financial Times described the quantum computing race as wide open. It is true that more companies are entering the field, each pursuing different technical paths and hoping to deliver a useful gate-model machine by the end of the decade. But expanding participation should not be confused with equal position. A small number of companies are clearly ahead. And if the question is who has delivered the first commercially viable, “useful” quantum computer, that line has already been crossed. By D-Wave. That is an important milestone to recognize on World Quantum Day 2026: quantum computing is no longer defined by possibility alone. It is increasingly defined by impact. What was once confined to physics labs and research papers is now being deployed against real operational problems. Today, the real race is not among quantum companies trying to prove relevance someday. It is among organizations deciding whether they will adopt quantum computing now or fall behind competitors that do. This shift is arriving exactly when the limits of classical computing are becoming impossible to ignore. AI is driving unprecedented demand for compute, energy, and infrastructure. Supply chains are becoming more volatile and costly. National security environments are growing more dynamic and data-intensive. Across industries and governments, leaders are running into problems that are too large, too complex, and too time-sensitive for classical approaches alone. Quantum computing is beginning to change that. Not as a replacement for classical computing, but as a powerful complement to classical systems and AI that can accelerate decision-making, improve resilience, and deliver new levels of performance. It is also important to be clear-eyed about the quantum computing technology landscape. Much of the industry remains focused solely on gate-model quantum computing. Gate-model will matter tremendously over time, especially in areas such as chemistry and simulation. But it is not the whole story, and it is not where commercial value is being delivered today. Annealing quantum computing addresses a different and equally important set of problems, especially optimization problems that sit at the center of modern business and government operations. It is the only quantum architecture delivering commercial value at scale now. This is why D-Wave stands apart. The D-Wave Difference D-Wave is the only company with a dual-platform strategy spanning both annealing and gate-model systems, positioning us to address the full range of customers’ complex computational problems. Our energy-efficient annealing quantum computers are delivering customer value today on real-world applications. At the same time, our dual-rail gate-model technology gives us a clear path to fault tolerance. By combining the speed of superconducting qubits with the fidelity associated with ion trap and neutral atom approaches, we are building something fundamentally different. As the market evolves, the field will not stay crowded forever. I believe that it will consolidate around the few companies that can demonstrate three things: 1. Real performance advantage 2. Meaningful commercial adoption 3. Scalable, economically viable architectures Many will not meet all three criteria. I believe that D-Wave already has. We are the only company to demonstrate quantum supremacy on a useful, real-world problem. One of the world’s most powerful classical supercomputers would have taken nearly one million years and consumed the equivalent of the world’s entire annual electricity consumption to solve the problem. Our Advantage2™ system solved it in minutes, using only $1 of electricity. We are the only company running production applications for Forbes Global 2000 enterprise customers. In fact, this year we signed a $10 million, two-year agreement with a Fortune 100 company — the largest quantum computing as a service deal in the industry’s history. And we are engaged with many of the world’s leading airlines, telecom operators, defense contractors, chemical companies, healthcare companies, aerospace companies, and more. Customers are no longer asking if quantum will be useful someday. They are asking us how fast they can put it to work. That is why World Quantum Day feels different this year. The Commercial Impact of Quantum Computing Is Already Here This is not just a moment to celebrate scientific promise. It is a moment to recognize commercial reality. It is also a moment to recognize the ecosystem making this progress possible: our community of customers, partners, developers, researchers, and advocates who believed early that D-Wave’s quantum computing technology could become practical, and who now see firsthand what it can do: Pattison Food Group uses our systems to automatically create weekly employee schedules, trimming what was once an 80-hour task to just 15 hours each week; an 80% reduction expected to save up to 50,000 workforce hours annually. Ford Otosan can now schedule the production of 1,000 transit vehicles in just five minutes instead of 30. AT&T used our technology to optimize its field technician dispatch in just 15 seconds vs. an hour. A collaboration with Davidson Technologies and Anduril Industries showed that our technology could compute a missile-defense solution 10x faster and mitigate 9-12% more threats than classical-only approaches. These are not theory projects. They are proof points. They show that quantum computing is already beginning to transform how organizations operate, compete, and respond to complexity. Up to now, World Quantum Day has been a celebration of what quantum computing might one day become. This year, it is increasingly a recognition of what quantum computing is already doing. And D-Wave intends to keep leading that transition. A version of this article originally appeared on LinkedIn. Dr. Alan Baratz Chief Executive Officer Dr. Alan Baratz became the CEO of D-Wave Quantum in 2020. Previously, as Executive Vice President of R&D and Chief Product Officer, he drove the development, delivery, and support of all of D-Wave’s products, technologies, and applications. He has over 25 years of experience in product development and bringing new products to market at leading technology companies and software startups. As the first president of JavaSoft at Sun Microsystems, Alan oversaw the growth and adoption of the Java platform from its infancy to a robust platform supporting mission-critical applications in nearly 80 percent of Fortune 1000 companies. He has also held executive positions at Symphony, Avaya, Cisco, and IBM. He served as CEO and president of Versata, Zaplet, and NeoPath Networks, and as a managing director at Warburg Pincus LLC. Alan holds a doctorate in computer science from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Share this article

Con Edison Asks Customers in Certain Areas of Queens, Brooklyn to Conserve Energy
summary: Company Reduces Voltage by 8 Percent to Maintain Reliability
body_text: Con Edison is asking customers in certain neighborhoods in Queens and Brooklyn to conserve energy while company crews repair equipment. Con Edison has also reduced voltage by 8 percent in the areas as a precaution to protect equipment and maintain service as repairs are completed. The equipment problems in these neighborhoods have no effect on the rest of the Con Edison system. Con Edison has asked customers in these areas not to use energy-intensive appliances such as washers, dryers, and microwaves until crews complete repairs. The company also asks customers to limit unnecessary use of air conditioning. If you have two air conditioners, use only one and set it to the highest comfortable temperature. The company also asks that drivers refrain from charging their electric vehicles in these areas, except when necessary. One area in Queens is bounded by the Brooklyn-Queens Expressway and 51st Avenue on the north, the Jackie Robinson Parkway on the south, Queens Boulevard on the east, and the Brooklyn borough line on the west. The area includes 116,600 customers in parts, or all, of these neighborhoods: Glendale, Forest Hills, Forest Hills Gardens, Ridgewood, Maspeth and Middle Village. A second area in Queens affected by voltage reduction covers an area bounded by Queens Plaza North on the north, 33rd Street on the east, Newtown Creek on the south, and the East River on the west. The area includes 17,000 customers in the Long Island City and Hunters Point neighborhoods. A third area in Queens is bounded by the Sunnyside Railroad Yards and Northern Boulevard on the north, 58th Street on the east, the Brooklyn-Queens Expressway on the south, and 33rd Street on the west. It includes the neighborhoods of Sunnyside, Sunnyside Gardens and Woodside. The area has about 35,000 customers who could be affected by voltage reduction. In Brooklyn, one area is bounded on the north by 3rd Street and 4th Street, by the Narrows and Gravesend Bay on the south, by Fort Hamilton Parkway and 5th Avenue on the east, and by Gowanus Bay and the Narrows on the west. The area includes 106,000 customers in parts, or all, of the following neighborhoods: Bay Ridge, Borough Park, Carroll Gardens, Dyker Heights, Park Slope and Sunset Park. Also, in Brooklyn voltage is being reduced in an area bounded on the north by Prospect Park and Greenwood Cemetery, on the south by Belt Parkway and Long Island Railroad (LIRR), on the east by 20th Avenue and Marlborough Road, and on the west by Fort Hamilton Parkway. The area includes 122,000 customers in parts, or all, of these neighborhoods: Windsor Terrace, Kensington, Flatbush, Borough Park, Bensonhurst, and Dyker Heights. Con Edison has asked customers in these areas not to use energy-intensive appliances such as washers, dryers, and microwaves until crews complete repairs. The company also asks customers to limit unnecessary use of air conditioning. If you have two air conditioners, use only one and set it to the highest comfortable temperature. The company also asks that drivers refrain from charging their electric vehicles in these areas, except when necessary. Customers can report outages and check service restoration status at www.conEd.com/reportoutage , or with our mobile app for iOS or Android devices, or by calling 1-800-75-CONED (1-800-752-6633). When calling, customers should report whether their neighbors also have lost power. Customers who report outages will receive updates with their estimated restoration times as they become available. Customers can follow Con Edison on X , Instagram or like us on Facebook for general outage updates, safety tips and storm preparation information. The company is in communication with New York City Emergency Management.

title: When to Set Up Formal AR vs. Just Using Stripe: A Decision Framework In 2026
summary: Stripe works great for early SaaS payments, but it’s not always enough once you introduce net terms, invoices, credits, disputes, or multi-channel billing. Use this decision framework to know when to keep it simple vs. implement a formal accounts receivable (AR) process.
body_text: Most SaaS startups start with Stripe and a bank account. That’s usually the right move. You can charge cards, send receipts, and reconcile deposits without building a finance workflow too early. The question is when “Stripe-only” starts creating avoidable work and cash leakage, and when it’s time to formalize accounts receivable (AR). Last verified: Jan 2026 What “Formal AR” Actually Means Formal AR is not a specific software. It’s a set of processes that make cash collection predictable and your books reconcilable. A formal AR setup usually includes: invoices that map cleanly to a general ledger an AR subledger or AR ledger account in your accounting system customer-level balances (open invoices, credits, unapplied cash) payment application rules (what payment applies to what invoice) dunning and collections workflows for past-due invoices month-end reconciliation that ties billing data to AR and revenue Stripe can support parts of this (invoices, payment links, dunning), but the decision depends on your billing model and operational needs. Stripe-Only Is Usually Fine If You Check These Boxes Staying “Stripe-only” is typically fine when: customers pay by card at purchase (no net terms) you don’t issue many invoices pricing is simple (one plan, no custom contracts) refunds and credits are rare you do not need customer-specific aging or collections workflows you can reconcile payouts to revenue without manual work If your workflow is “charge card → Stripe payout → record revenue,” you can keep it lean for a while. Stripe’s invoicing and billing tools can support basic invoicing and subscription workflows if you want to stay within Stripe: Stripe Invoicing and Stripe Billing . Formal AR Becomes Worth It When Any of These Are True These are the common triggers for moving beyond Stripe-only. You offer net terms or invoice-based billing If you have Net 15 / Net 30 customers, you need: a clear invoice process a way to track what is open vs paid a consistent follow-up cadence Once you have invoices that are not immediately paid, you have AR, whether you call it that or not. You have more than one payment channel Stripe is one channel. The moment you add: ACH/wires initiated outside Stripe marketplace payouts reseller collections invoices paid via checks …Stripe stops being a complete AR system. You need a place where all payments and invoices converge. You use credits, adjustments, or partial payments Credits and partial payments are where “simple” breaks. Examples: customer prepays annually, then downgrades mid-term you issue a credit for downtime customer pays multiple invoices in one wire customer short-pays an invoice and asks for an adjustment If you don’t have rules for applying cash and credits, you end up with mismatched balances and customer confusion. You have meaningful disputes, chargebacks, or refunds Disputes change how you run AR: you need to track disputed amounts separately you need a consistent evidence process you need refund and chargeback visibility in close Stripe handles dispute workflows, but finance still needs clean classification and reconciliation on the ledger side. You’re spending too much time reconciling payouts If close includes recurring questions like: “Why does Stripe deposits not match invoices?” “Which invoices were paid in this payout?” “Are these payments applied to the right customer?” …you’re paying the complexity tax every month. Stripe payouts include multiple transactions net of fees, refunds, disputes, and timing differences, which can make accounting reconciliation non-trivial as volume grows: Stripe payouts documentation . You need investor- or audit-ready financials As you approach diligence or audit, you want: AR aging you can defend revenue and AR that tie to contracts and invoices consistent cutoffs at period end This is also where revenue recognition concepts start to matter. Contract assets, AR, and deferred revenue are distinct concepts under ASC 606 frameworks, even if you keep reporting simple early on: FASB Topic 606 update (ASU 2016-10) PDF . A Practical Decision Scorecard Use this as a quick “do we need formal AR” check. Stay Stripe-only (or mostly Stripe) if: fewer than 10 invoice-paying customers most customers pay immediately by card refunds and credits are infrequent you rarely need partial payments or manual adjustments you can close monthly without AR reconciliation issues Move toward formal AR if: you have enterprise or mid-market customers with net terms you are issuing invoices that can be paid outside Stripe you offer credits, usage adjustments, or mid-term plan changes you need customer-level aging and collections you spend hours per month reconciling Stripe to the ledger you are preparing for financing, audit, or more complex revenue recognition If you are in the middle, the best approach is often “lightweight AR” first: keep Stripe for payments, but implement an AR workflow in your accounting system with consistent invoicing, payment application, and reconciliation. What a Lightweight AR Setup Looks Like (Before You Overbuild) A good “Phase 1” AR setup usually includes: an invoice template with clear service period, due date, and payment instructions one AR account in the GL a single clearing account for Stripe activity (optional but helpful) basic aging buckets (current, 1–30, 31–60, 61–90, 90+) a weekly collections routine for past-due invoices You can keep this simple, but it needs to be consistent. The IRS also emphasizes maintaining supporting documents for business transactions and organizing records so you can prepare financial statements and tax returns. Invoices and payment records are part of that trail: IRS recordkeeping overview . Common Mistakes When “Upgrading” AR Treating AR as a tool decision, not a process decision Buying an AR tool does not fix: unclear billing terms inconsistent invoice timing missing service periods unclear credit/refund policy Fix the process first, then choose tooling. Mixing cash basis thinking with invoice thinking When you invoice on net terms, you need to track what you are owed, not just what hit the bank. If your books are still “bank balance accounting,” AR will always feel wrong. Not defining how to apply payments You need a default rule: apply payments to the oldest open invoice first, unless remittance instructions specify otherwise If you don’t define this, you create a permanent “unapplied cash” problem. Not documenting refunds, credits, and disputes Refunds and credits should be visible and consistently classified. Otherwise your AR aging becomes unreliable. Migration Plan: Stripe-Only to Formal AR Without Chaos A clean migration can be done in four steps: standardize invoice numbering and invoice terms create a single source of truth for open invoices (AR ledger) implement a payment application workflow (including wires/ACH outside Stripe) reconcile Stripe payouts through a clearing approach or a consistent mapping to invoices and fees Stripe provides reporting exports and payout data that can support reconciliation workflows if you keep Stripe as a payment rail: Stripe reporting and Stripe balance and transactions . Where Afternoon Fits If you want to keep Stripe for payments but move to a finance workflow that supports invoices, net terms, customer balances, credits, payment application, and month-end reconciliation, Afternoon offers an AR product that ties invoicing and collections into your general ledger and close process. Summary Topic Details Stripe-only works when mostly card payments, few invoices, minimal credits/refunds, easy reconciliation You need formal AR when net terms, invoice billing, multi-channel payments, credits/adjustments, heavy reconciliation, diligence/audit readiness Lightweight AR first invoice standardization, GL AR account, aging, weekly collections routine Biggest pitfalls unclear terms, no payment application rules, messy refunds/credits, treating it as only a tool choice Migration approach standardize invoicing, centralize open invoices, define payment application, reconcile Stripe consistently Official References Stripe Invoicing Stripe Billing Stripe payouts documentation Stripe reporting Stripe balance and transactions IRS recordkeeping overview FASB Topic 606 update (ASU 2016-10) PDF
